title: Hershey ends gubernatorial bid exploration, refiles for Senate seat
summary: Sen. Stephen S. Hershey's contemplation of a run for governor ended quietly Friday, when he filed for reelection to his current seat, months after forming a committee to explore a possible run for the 2026 GOP gubernatorial nomination.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters February 22, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters February 22, 2026

Sen. Stephen S. Hershey’s contemplation of a run for governor ended quietly Friday.

Hershey, a senator from the Upper Shore since October 2014, announced in September he was forming a committee to explore a possible run for the 2026 Republican nomination for governor.  Such a campaign would have required him to forgo running for the Senate.

In the end, Hershey opted to seek re-election to the Senate. Hershey filed Friday for his current seat. He did not issue a statement on the move and was not immediately available for comment.

Hershey toyed with the idea of running for governor in the days following the announcement by Ed Hale, a longtime Democrat, that he would switch parties and run for the Republican nomination. The announcement irritated Hershey, who called Hale a political opportunist.

“Republicans know the difference between conviction and convenience,” Hershey said at the time.

But a run by Hershey seemed a long shot. Larry Hogan, the last Republican elected governor in Maryland, spent four years laying the groundwork for his first run for governor in 2014. Hershey did not have the same exposure outside his rural district that a run for governor would have required.

Had he gone through with it, Hershey would have been joining an already crowded field of Republican hopefuls seeking the nomination for governor. In addition to Hale, who announced his running mate, Tyrone Keys Jr., Thursday and officially filed Friday, there are seven other gubernatorial tickets signed up for the GOP primary. They include John Myrick, who has been running for almost a year now, and Dan Cox, the 2022 nominee who lost to Gov. Wes Moore by a 2-to-1 margin.

Hogan, who was long talked about as a potential 2026 challenger to Moore, announced in January that he will not run.
